Commentary of al-Zamakhshari (al-Kashshaf) on surah 74, verses 1–5:

Makkiyya, and it has fifty-six verses [revealed after al-Muzzammil]. In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful.

Al-Muddaththir (ﷺ, "the one wrapped up") means one who wears a dithar (wrapping cloth), which is what is above the shi'ar (undergarment): it is the garment that is closest to the body. From it is the saying of the Prophet (ﷺ): "The Ansar are the shi'ar (undergarment) and the people are the dithar (outer garment)" [[This was mentioned previously in Al 'Imran.]] It is also said that this is the first surah to be revealed. Jabir ibn 'Abd Allah narrated from the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ): "I was on Mount Hira', and I was called: 'O Muhammad, you are the Messenger of Allah.' So I looked to my right and my left and saw nothing. Then I looked above me and saw something" [[Agreed upon (by al-Bukhari and Muslim), from the narration of Abu Salama from him, and more complete than this.]]. In the narration of 'A'isha: "I looked above me and suddenly he was sitting on a throne between the heaven and the earth — meaning the angel who had called to him. I was terrified and returned to Khadija and said: 'Wrap me up, wrap me up!' Then Jibril descended and said: 'O you who are wrapped up (al-muddaththir).'"

From al-Zuhri: the first thing revealed was the surah "Read in the name of your Lord" up to His words "what he did not know." The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) was grieved and began to climb the highest mountains. Then Jibril came to him and said: "You are the Prophet of Allah." So he returned to Khadija and said: "Wrap me up and pour cold water over me." Then it was revealed: "O you who are wrapped up" [[Al-Tabari narrated it through Muhammad ibn Thawr from Ma'mar from al-Zuhri, who said: "The first thing revealed to the Prophet (ﷺ) was 'Read' — and he mentioned it and went further than this. Al-Hakim narrated it through the route of Muhammad ibn Sirin from al-Zuhri from 'Urwa from 'A'isha, may Allah be pleased with her.]]. It is also said: he heard from the Quraysh what he disliked, so he grieved and covered himself with his garment in thought, as the one who is grieved does. So he was commanded not to abandon warning them, even if they made him hear (what he disliked) and harmed him.

From 'Ikrima that he recited it with the form of the passive participle: "min dathharahu" (the one wrapped up), and he said: "I have been wrapped up in this matter, and it has been bound upon you," just as He said in al-Muzzammil: "Arise from your resting place." Or (it means) "arise with a resolve and determination."

"Then warn" — so warn your people of the punishment of Allah if they do not believe. The correct meaning is: carry out the warning without restricting it to anyone in particular.

"And your Lord, then magnify" — single out your Lord with magnification, which is describing Him with greatness (kibriya'), and saying: "Allah is greatest" (Allahu akbar). It is narrated that when this was revealed, the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Allahu akbar," and Khadija magnified Him too and rejoiced, and became certain that it was revelation. It may also be taken to refer to the takbir of prayer. The fa' (then) has entered to convey the meaning of a condition, as if it were said: "Whatever the case, do not neglect to magnify Him."

"And your garments, then purify" — a command that his garments be free of impurities (najasat), because purity of garments is a condition of prayer, which is not valid without it; and it is preferable and more beloved outside of prayer too, and it is unbecoming for a good believer to carry filth. It is also said: it is a command to shorten them, and to oppose the Arabs in their lengthening of garments and trailing of their skirts, since that is something with which one cannot be safe from encountering impurities. It is also said: it is a command to purify the self from what is loathsome in actions and disgraceful in customs. It is said: "So-and-so has pure garments and a pure collar, skirt and sleeves," when they describe him as free from faults and blemishes of character. And "so-and-so has soiled garments" refers to a treacherous man. This is because a garment clings to a person and encloses him, so it is used as a metaphor for him. Do you not see their saying: "Zayd's garment pleased me," just as they say: "Zayd's intellect and character pleased me"? And they say: "Glory is in his garment, and generosity is under his robe." Also, because it is generally the case that one whose inner self is purified and cleansed is concerned with purifying and cleansing the outer self, and refuses anything but avoiding filth and preferring purity in everything.

"And the rujz" — it is read with kasra and with damma. It means the punishment, and its meaning is: abandon what leads to it, such as the worship of idols and other sins. The meaning is: persist in abandoning it, since he was innocent of it.

Commentary of al-Zamakhshari (al-Kashshaf) on surah 74, verse 6–7:

Al-Hasan recited: ﴿wa-la tamunn﴾. "Tastakthir" is in the accusative position of a circumstantial clause (ḥāl), meaning: do not give while seeing what you give as much, or seeking much in return. He forbade al-istighzār (seeking a greater return), which is to give something while hoping to receive from the recipient more than what was given, and this is permissible. From this is the hadith: "The one who seeks a greater return is rewarded for his gift." [[Mentioned earlier in al-Rum, from the statement of Shurayh.]] In this there are two views. The first is that it is a prohibition specific to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), because Allah the Exalted chose for him the noblest manners and the finest character. The second is that it is a prohibition of disapproval (tanzīh), not of prohibition (taḥrīm), for him and for his community.

Al-Hasan also recited: ﴿tastakthir﴾ with a sukūn. There are three possible readings of this. The first is substitution (ibdāl) from ﴿tamunn﴾, as if it were said: "Do not bestow [favour], that you may not regard it as much," taking it from al-mann (reproach) in the words of the Mighty and Majestic: ﴿Those who spend their wealth in the way of Allah, then do not follow what they have spent with reproach (mann) or injury﴾ [2:262], because it is the nature of one who reproaches for what he gives that he regards it as much, i.e., sees it as abundant and counts it great. The second is that it is lightened by sukūn for ease, like one who says Thurw with a sukūn on the ʿaḍud. The third is that it is considered in the state of pause (waqf).

Al-A'mash recited it in the accusative, with the particle "an" (that) elided and implied, as in the verse:

*Ala ayyuha al-zājiri aḥḍara al-wughā*
[[The explanation of this witness was given in the first part, page 159, so refer to it if you wish. Its corrector.]]

This is supported by the reading of Ibn Mas'ud: ﴿wa-la tamunn an tastakthir﴾. In the nominative it is permissible for "an" to be omitted while its government is nullified, as is narrated: *Ahḍara al-wughā* with the nominative. ﴿And for your Lord, be patient﴾ [74:7], and for the sake of Allah's countenance, so employ patience. It was said: over the harm of the polytheists. It was said: over performing the obligatory duties. And from al-Nakha'i: over your giving, as if he connected it to what precedes it, making it patience in giving without seeking much in return. The apt view is that it is a command to the act itself, and that it encompasses in general every matter to be endured and every matter to be endured from, and that the patience over the harm of the disbelievers is intended, since it is one of the things the general expression includes.

In the nominative it is permissible for "an" to be omitted while its government is nullified, as is narrated: *Ahḍara al-wughā* with the nominative. ﴿And for your Lord, be patient﴾ [74:7], and for the sake of Allah's countenance, so employ patience. It was said: over the harm of the polytheists. It was said: over performing the obligatory duties. And from al-Nakha'i: over your giving, as if he connected it to what precedes it, making it patience in giving without seeking much in return. The apt view is that it is a command to the act itself, and that it encompasses in general every matter to be endured and every matter to be endured from, and that the patience over the harm of the disbelievers is intended, since it is one of the things the general expression includes.

"And the fa' in His saying, ﴿So when the trumpet is sounded﴾, marks causation, as if He had said: Be patient over their harm, for before them is a grievous day, in which they will meet the consequence of their harm, and in which the consequence of your patience over it will be met. The fa' in ﴿Then that﴾ marks the apodosis (jaza').

If you ask: With what is idha (ʿidha, "when") in the accusative, and how is it valid for yawma'idhin (yawma'idhin, "that day") to be a complement (zarf) of yawmun ʿasir (yawmun ʿasir, "a grievous day")? I answer: idha is in the accusative governed by what the apodosis (jaza', "the response clause") indicates, because the meaning is: ﴿When the trumpet is sounded in the trumpet, the matter will be grievous for the disbelievers.﴾ What permits yawma'idhin to be a complement of yawmun ʿasir is that the meaning is: ﴿That is the time of the sounding,﴾ the occurrence of a grievous day, since the Day of Resurrection comes and takes place at the moment the trumpet (al-naqur, "the trumpet") is sounded. It has been disputed whether it is the first blast or the second blast. It is also permissible for yawma'idhin to be indeclinable (mabni) and in the nominative position, as a substitution (badal) for ﴿that﴾, with yawmun ʿasir as the predicate, as if it were said: ﴿So the day of the sounding is a grievous day.﴾

If you ask: What is the benefit of His saying ﴿not easy﴾ (ghayr yasir) when ʿasir (ʿasir, "grievous") would suffice in its place? I answer: When He said ʿala al-kafirin (ʿala al-kafirin, "upon the disbelievers"), restricting the grievousness to them, He said ghayr yasir (ghayr yasir, "not easy") to indicate that it will not be upon them as it is upon the believers, an easy and light matter, so as to combine the threat to the disbelievers with an increase in their anger, and the glad tidings and consolation to the believers.

It is also permissible that what is meant is that it is grievous, with no hope that it will return to being easy, just as the hope exists that the difficulties of worldly affairs may become easy.

**Wahidan** (وَحِيداً) is a circumstantial accusative (ḥāl) and may refer to God, exalted and mighty, in two senses. The first: ﴿Leave Me with the one I created alone﴾ (74:11). I will suffice you in taking vengeance on him against every avenger. The second: I created him alone, and none shared with Me in his creation. Alternatively, it is a circumstantial accusative referring to the created person, meaning: I created him while he was solitary, unique, with no wealth and no children, like His saying ﴿And you have come to Us alone, as We created you the first time﴾ (6:94).

It was said that this was revealed concerning al-Walid ibn al-Mughira al-Makhzumi, who was called "the Solitary" (al-Wahid) among his people. Perhaps he was given that title after the revelation of this verse. But if he was called by it before, then the verse is a mockery of him and of his title, and a diversion of it from the purpose for which they used it. They used it to praise him and to commend him as the unique one of his people, for his leadership, wealth and eminence in this world, and the verse turns it into blame and reproach: he was created alone, with no wealth and no children. Then God gave him that, and he disbelieved in God's blessing, associated partners with Him, and mocked His religion.

**Mamdudan** (مَمْدُوداً) means extended, spread out, abundant. Or it means increasing, from madda al-nahr (the river was supplied) and madda nahran akhar (one river supplied another). It was said: he had crops, livestock and trade. From Ibn Abbas: it is what he had between Mecca and al-Ta'if of various kinds of wealth. It was said: he had an orchard in al-Ta'if whose fruit did not cease in summer or winter.

It was said: he had a thousand mithqals. It was said: four thousand. It was said: nine thousand. It was said: a million. From Ibn Jurayj: the yield of one month following another.

**Wa banina shuhudan** (وَبَنِينَ شُهُوداً): sons who were present, attending him in Mecca and not leaving him, for managing work or trade. This is because they were sufficed by their father's abundant blessing and were free from earning and seeking their own livelihood. So he was at ease with them, his heart not preoccupied by their absence, nor by fear of the dangers of travel for them, and he did not grieve over their separation or long for them. It is also permissible that the meaning is: they were men who attended with him assemblies and gatherings, or whose testimony was heard in matters brought before judgment. From Mujahid: he had ten sons. It was said: thirteen. It was said: seven, all of them men: al-Walid ibn al-Walid, Khalid, Amara, Hisham, al-As, Qays and Abd Shams. Three of them embraced Islam: Khalid, Hisham and Amara.

**Wa mahhadtu lahu tamhidan** (وَمَهَّدْتُ لَهُ تَمْهِيداً): I spread out for him a wide standing and leadership among his people. So I completed My blessing upon him, with wealth and standing, and the combination of the two, which is perfection in the view of worldly people. From it comes the people's saying: "May God make your support and your standing endure," meaning an increase in rank and dignity. Al-Walid was among the notables and chieftains of Quraysh, and for this reason he was called "the Solitary" and "the Basil of Quraysh."

**Thumma yatma'u** (ثُمَّ يَطْمَعُ): this expresses astonishment and disapproval of his greed and eagerness. [[Mahmud said: "I entered thumma (ثم) to indicate astonishment at his greed and his eagerness for more, and disapproval of that. So God returned his greed disappointed..." etc. Ahmad said: because the shameful word occurred to his mind after he had reflected, he could not restrain himself from uttering it without delay.]] The meaning is that there is no increase beyond the abundance and multitude that he was given.

It was said that he used to say: "If Muhammad is truthful, then Paradise was created only for me."

**Kalla** (كَلَّا): a rebuke to him and a cutting off of his hope and greed. **Innahu kana li-ayatina 'anidan** (إِنَّهُ كانَ لِآياتِنا عَنِيداً): this is an explanation of the rebuke, given as a resumptive clause (istinaf), as if someone had asked: why is he not given more? So it was said: he opposed the signs of the Bestower and thereby disbelieved in His blessing, and the disbeliever does not deserve more. It is reported that after the revelation of this verse, he continued to decline in his wealth until he died.

**Sa-urhiquhu saudan** (سَأُرْهِقُهُ صَعُوداً): I will cover him with a steep ascent, a difficult climb. This is a figure for the painful punishment he will suffer, which is unbearable. From the Prophet (ﷺ): "He will be made to climb a steep ascent in the Fire. Whenever he places his hand on it, it melts; when he lifts it, it returns; and when he places his foot on it, it melts; when he lifts it, it returns." And from him (peace be upon him): "As-su'ud is a mountain of fire. One climbs in it for seventy autumns, then falls down in it, and so on forever."

**Innahu fakkara** (إِنَّهُ فَكَّرَ): this is an explanation of the threat. It is as if God hastened to him poverty after wealth and humiliation after honour in this world because of his obstinacy, and will punish him in the Hereafter with the most severe and dreadful torment, because in his obstinacy he reached the furthest extent of his reflection, including his calling the Qur'an sorcery. It is also permissible that the word of rebuke is followed by **sa-urhiquhu saudan** as a refutation of his claim that Paradise was created only for him, and as a statement that he is among the people of the Fire who will suffer the most severe punishment. His obstinacy is given as the reason, and **innahu fakkara** (إِنَّهُ فَكَّرَ) is then a substitute (badal) for **innahu kana li-ayatina 'anidan** (إِنَّهُ كانَ لِآياتِنا عَنِيداً), clarifying his obstinacy. Its meaning is: he reflected on what he would say about the Qur'an, **wa qaddara** (وَقَدَّرَ), and determined within himself what to say and prepared it.

**Faqutila kayfa qaddara** (فَقُتِلَ كَيْفَ قَدَّرَ): this is an expression of wonder at his determination and at his hitting the target in it, and his striking the mark that Quraysh were aiming at. Or it is praise of him in the manner of mockery. Or it is a quotation of what they kept repeating: "Killed, how he determined!" mocking them and their admiration of his determination, and their magnification of his words.

The meaning of the speaker's saying, "May God kill him, how brave he is! May God disgrace him, how perceptive he is!" is to indicate that he has reached the level which makes him worthy of envy, and his envier prays against him with such words.

It is reported that al-Walid said to Banu Makhzum: "By God, I have just heard from Muhammad words that are neither the words of humans nor the words of jinn. Indeed, there is sweetness in it, and radiance upon it. Its upper part is fruitful, its lower part is abundant; it rises and nothing rises above it." Quraysh said: "By God, al-Walid has apostatized (ṣabā'a, صبأ). By God, all of Quraysh will apostatize!" Abu Jahl said: "I will suffice you against him." So he sat with him, sorrowful, and spoke to him with words that angered him. Then he (al-Walid) got up and came to them and said: "You claim that Muhammad is mad. Have you seen him choke? You claim he is a soothsayer. Have you ever seen him divine? You claim he is a poet. Have you ever seen him engage in poetry? You claim he is a liar. Have you ever tested him in any lie?" To all of that they said: "No, by God." Then they said: "So what is he?" He reflected, then said: "He is nothing but a sorcerer. Have you not seen how he separates a man from his wife, his child and his clients? What he says is nothing but sorcery which he has transmitted from Musaylima and the people of Babylon." The assembly erupted with joy, and they dispersed admiring his words and marveling at him.

**Thumma nazara fi wujuh al-nas** (ثُمَّ نَظَرَ فِي وُجُوهِ النَّاسِ) [[The phrase "thumma nazara fi wujuh al-nas" means he looked with the corner of his eye, out of arrogance or anger, as in al-Sihah. (A)]], **thumma qatata wajhahu** (ثُمَّ قَطَّبَ وَجْهَهُ) [[The phrase "thumma qatata wajhahu": in al-Sihah, qatata wajhahu taqtiban means he frowned. Also there: 'abasa 'ubusan kalaha, and basara busuran: kalaha. It is said: 'abasa and basara. (A)]], then he turned back and went off in haste, showing arrogance, when the shameful word occurred to his mind and he was about to cast it out, shaping his features in the manner in which he shaped them until he devised what he devised, mocking him. It was said: he weighed what he would say, then looked at it, then frowned when his stratagems ran out and he did not know what to say. It was also said: he frowned at the face of the Messenger of God (ﷺ), then turned away from the truth and was arrogant towards it, and said what he said.

**Thumma nazara** (ثُمَّ نَظَرَ) is conjoined (ʿaṭf) to **fakkara** (فَكَّرَ) and **qaddara** (وَقَدَّرَ), and the imprecation (al-du'a') is an interjection (i'tiraḍ) between them.

If you ask: what is the meaning of **thumma** (ثُمَّ) when it enters into the repetition of the imprecation? I say: it indicates that the second occurrence is more eloquent than the first. A similar example is the line of poetry: "Ah, O Asma, peace! Then peace! Then peace!" (ألا يا أسلمي ثمّ أسلمي ثمّت أسلمي).

If you ask: what is the meaning of **thumma** placed between the verbs that follow it? I say: it indicates that it occurs in reflection and deliberation, and as if there is a delay and a distance between the consecutive actions.

If you ask: why is it said **fa-qala inna hadha** (فَقالَ إِنْ هذا), with **fa** (فَ), after the preceding clauses were conjoined with **thumma** (ثُمَّ)? I say: because the word occurred to his mind after the search, and he could not restrain himself from uttering it without delay.

If you ask: why was no conjunction particle placed between the two clauses? I say: because the latter stands in relation to the former as emphasis (tawkīd) stands to what it emphasizes.

**Commentary of al-Zamakhshari (al-Kashshaf) on Surah 74, verses 26–31:**

﴿I will burn him in Saqar﴾. ﻿(Saqar is) a substitute (badal, apposition) for ﴿I will overwhelm him with arduous torment﴾. It leaves nothing that is cast into it without destroying it, and when it has destroyed it, it does not leave it, but it is restored (to be destroyed again). Or: it does not leave anything alone, nor does it let it go from destruction; rather, everything cast into it is inevitably destroyed. ﴿Scorching to the skin﴾, from the blaze of the midday heat (lawwaha min lawh al-hajir). He said:

*"She says, 'What has the traveller's journey withered you?' O daughter of my uncle, the noonday heat has withered me."*

[[The heat withered him (lawwahahu al-harr lawhan): it changed his colour and blackened him. Al-hajira is the intensity of heat. Ahjara al-qawm and hajjaru (with the doubled letter) and tahajjaru: they travelled in the midday heat. In this there is iltifat (a shift in address): it is as if he first addressed someone other than her. *Mathalan* (a parable) is a specification (tamyiz) for this, or a circumstantial accusative (hal) from it, like His saying: ﴿This is God's she-camel, a sign for you﴾.

If you say: Why did they call it a *mathal*?

I say: It is a metaphor (isti'ara) drawn from the proverb (mathal mudrab), because it is of what is strange and novel in speech. They regard this number as strange and unprecedented. The meaning is: "What did God intend by this strange number, and what purpose did He aim at in making the angels nineteen rather than twenty, or the same?" Their purpose was to deny it from its root, and to say that it is not from God, and that if it were from God it would not have come with this deficient number.

The *kaf* in ﴿Thus﴾ is in the accusative, and *dhalika* refers to what precedes it, the meaning of misguidance and guidance. That is: "Like that mentioned misguidance and guidance, He leads astray the disbelievers and guides the believers." That is, He does a good deed founded on wisdom and rightness, so the believers see it as wisdom and submit to it, believing that all of God's acts are good and wise, and this increases them in faith; while the disbelievers deny it and doubt. In it, He increases them in disbelief and error.

﴿And none knows the hosts of your Lord except Him﴾: what is with Him of every kind of soldier, some of them in a complete number and some in a deficient number. The wisdom in the particular number of each host is known only to Him, and there is no way for anyone to know that, just as one does not know the wisdom in the number of the heavens and the earths, the days of the year, the months, the zodiacal signs, the stars, the numbers of the rites, the prescribed limits, the expiations, and the prayers in the Law. Or: "And none knows the hosts of your Lord, because of their great multitude, except Him. So it is not hard for Him to complete the guardians to twenty; but He has in this particular number a wisdom that you do not know, while He knows it." It was also said: this is an answer to the statement of Abu Jahl: "Does the Lord of Muhammad have helpers only nineteen?" And (the sentence) ﴿And We have not made the companions of the Fire ... except Him﴾ is a parenthetical clause (i'tiraḍ).

And His saying ﴿And it is nothing but a reminder to mankind﴾ is connected to the description of Saqar, and "it" refers to it (Saqar): that is, "Saqar and its description are nothing but a reminder to mankind." Or it refers to the verses in which it is mentioned.

Kallā (No!). This is a denial, after He made it (the Fire) a reminder, that it should be a reminder for them, because they do not take heed. Or it is a rebuke to whoever denies that one of the greatest calamities (ihdā al-kubar) is a warner.

It is also said: it is from "dabar al-layl al-nahār" (the night's turning back on the day), when it leaves it behind.

It is read "idh adbar."

"Al-kubar" is the plural of "al-kubrā," the alif of femininity being treated like its tā' (the plural pattern is formed as with a feminine noun).[[His saying "the alif of femininity being treated like its tā'" is perhaps "like its tā'" (A)]] When the pattern fu'la is pluralized as fu'al, the pattern fu'lā is also pluralized upon it. **Rahīnah** is not the feminine of **rahīn**. [[Maḥmūd said: "And it is not the feminine of rahīn…" Aḥmad said: Because it is fa‘īl in the sense of maf‘ūl, its masculine and feminine forms are the same, like qatīl and jadīd.]] It is used in His saying ﴿Every soul is held in pledge for what it has earned﴾, where it agrees with **al-nafs** (the soul). Had it been meant as an adjective, it would have been **rahīn**, since fa‘īl in the sense of maf‘ūl takes the same form for masculine and feminine. Rather, it is a noun meaning "pledge (rahn)," like **al-shatīmah** meaning **al-shatm** (insult). It is as if it were said: "Every soul is a pledge for what it has earned." From this is the line of poetry in the **Ḥamāsah** (anthology):

*Is it after the one at the slope of Na‘f Kuwaykib*
*is held in the grave of one with dust and gravel?*

[[Verse attributed to Musawwar ibn Ziyādah al-Ḥārithī. It is also said to be by ‘Abd al-Raḥmān ibn Zayd, whose father Ziyādah was killed, and he was offered seven blood-wealths for him, but he refused except to seek revenge.

*Shall I mention, out of forbearance toward the one who struck me,*
*and my forbearance that I strive without swearing?*

The interrogative here is one of denial. **Al-Na‘f** (with a fatḥah) means a mountain or an elevated place; it is also said to mean what faces you of a mountain. **Kuwaykib** is the name of a specific mountain. In this there is a substitution of detail after generality, which indicates the magnification of the place and the situation, i.e., "Is it after the killing of my father, who is buried in that place, while he is confined in a grave?" It is also said that **rahīnah** is in the genitive as a substitute for **alladhī**, and so it is a noun attached to the non-derived nouns in meaning "pledge (rahn)." It is said: "I buried the thing (ramastu al-shay’ ramsan)" when I put it in the dirt, so the verbal noun is used and its place is meant, which is the grave. **Al-Jandal** means stones. The interrogative hamzah is repeated in "a-udhkuru" as an emphasis of the first, because it governs this verb also in implication. It is possible that it governs an implied element, i.e., "Is it after my father that I rejoice in the blood-money?" It is also transmitted as "udhkira" with the doubling and passive form, so the first hamzah governs it, and there is no evidence in it then. **Al-Baqyā** means sparing something, i.e., "I do not mention among people that I spared the killer of my father," while my sparing him is with me striving and determined to kill him, not swearing to that, because I do not need to swear in carrying out my affairs. Or [it means] not falling short in striving, because **al-ii’lāt** comes in the sense of swearing and in the sense of falling short.]] It is as if he said: "a pledge of a grave." The meaning: every soul is held in pledge with God for what it has earned, not released, **except the companions of the right** (﴿except the companions of the right﴾), for they have freed their necks from it by what they made good from their earnings, just as the one who redeems a pledge releases it by paying the right.

It is reported from ‘Alī (may God be pleased with him) that he explained "the companions of the right" as children, because they have no deeds by which they are held in pledge. It is reported from Ibn ‘Abbās (may God be pleased with them both) that they are the angels.

﴿In gardens﴾, that is, they are in gardens whose description cannot be grasped, ﴿asking one another about the guilty﴾, one asking another about them. [[Maḥmūd said: "They ask one another about them, i.e., one asks another about them…" Aḥmad said: He only introduced the question as a pretext and a device to burden the verse with the indication that Muslim sinners, such as those who abandon prayer, will enter the Fire and remain eternally with the disbelievers. From the Messenger of God ﷺ: "Whoever recites Surah al-Muddaththir, God will give him ten good deeds for each person who believed in Muhammad and denied him in Mecca." [(Note): Narrated by al-Tha'labi, Ibn Mardawayh and al-Wahidi with their chains to Ubayy ibn Ka'b.]
